title: The Logic of the Herd
text:
Vaccination is usually thought of as a private decision: a parent protects a child, an adult protects himself. But vaccines also work at the level of whole communities. When a large enough share of people are immune to a contagious disease, the germ struggles to find new hosts. Each infected person passes it on to fewer others, and outbreaks fade before they can spread widely. This effect is known as herd immunity.

Herd immunity matters most for people who cannot be protected directly. Newborn babies may be too young for certain vaccines; some patients with weakened immune systems cannot safely receive them; and in a small number of people a vaccine simply fails to produce strong protection. These individuals depend on those around them. If their neighbours, classmates and relatives are immune, the disease is unlikely to reach them.

The protection is, however, fragile. The share of the population that must be immune varies from one disease to another, and highly contagious infections such as measles require very high coverage. If vaccination rates slip, even by a few points, gaps open in the community’s defences, and a single imported case can ignite an outbreak. Such falls often follow the spread of rumours about vaccine safety, or simply complacency in places where a disease has not been seen for years.

For this reason, public health officials argue that choosing to be vaccinated is a civic act as well as a personal one. Every immunised person helps to build a shield that protects the most vulnerable members of society.

title: The Map and the Pump
text:
For much of the nineteenth century, many doctors believed that diseases such as cholera were spread by foul air rising from rubbish and marshes. The theory seemed sensible: epidemics were worst in crowded, filthy districts where the smell was unbearable. Cleaning the air, rather than the water, appeared to be the answer.

During one outbreak in London, a physician who doubted this explanation decided to examine the evidence street by street. He marked on a map the homes of those who had died and noticed that the deaths clustered around a single public water pump. Several households further away had also been struck, but on inquiry he found that they, too, had drawn water from that pump because they preferred its taste. Just as telling were the exceptions: workers at a nearby brewery, who drank largely what the brewery produced, were mostly spared.

He persuaded the local authorities to remove the handle of the pump. His conclusion was not universally accepted at the time, and the germ responsible for cholera was not yet widely recognised. Nevertheless, his method of gathering cases, plotting them and searching for a common source became one of the foundations of modern epidemiology.

The episode carries a lesson beyond medicine. Theories, however respectable, must yield to careful observation. The physician did not possess an instrument that could reveal the culprit; he had only patience, a map and a willingness to ask where people drew their water.

title: The Scarcity of Attention
text:
For most of history, information was scarce. Books were expensive, newspapers reached few villages, and a curious person might travel for days to consult a single learned teacher. Today the problem has been turned upside down. A telephone that fits in a pocket gives access to more text, images and video than anyone could absorb in a thousand lifetimes. What has become scarce is not information but the attention needed to make sense of it.

This shift has created a new kind of competition. Websites, applications and broadcasters earn money when people look at them, so they are designed to capture and hold our gaze. Notifications arrive at irregular intervals, headlines are written to provoke, and endless feeds remove any natural point at which to stop. None of this is necessarily sinister, but its combined effect is to break the day into fragments.

The cost is felt most in activities that demand sustained concentration. Reading a long argument, solving a difficult problem or listening closely to another person all require the mind to stay with one thing for a while. When attention is constantly interrupted, such tasks become harder, and people may begin to prefer information that is short, emotional and easy to digest.

The answer is not to reject technology, which has brought immense benefits, but to use it deliberately. Turning off unnecessary alerts, setting aside hours for uninterrupted work and choosing sources for their quality rather than their volume are small habits. Taken together, they allow a person to remain the master of his tools rather than their servant.

title: What the Machine Does Not Know
text:
Programs that write fluent paragraphs, answer questions and summarise documents in seconds have moved from research laboratories into everyday life. To many users they seem almost to think. Yet the way most of these systems work is quite different from human understanding. They are trained on enormous collections of text and learn to predict which words are likely to follow others. From these patterns they can produce answers that sound confident and well informed.

Sounding informed, however, is not the same as being right. Because such a system generates what is statistically plausible, it can produce statements that are false but convincingly phrased, and it may even invent sources that do not exist. It does not, in the ordinary sense, check its claims against the world. A student who copies its output without verification may therefore hand in an essay that is polished in style and wrong in substance.

None of this means the technology is useless. Used carefully, it can draft letters, explain difficult concepts in simpler language, translate passages and help programmers find errors. Its value lies in speeding up work that a knowledgeable person can then review. The danger arises when people treat it as an authority rather than as an assistant.

The spread of these tools may therefore make human judgement more important, not less. The ability to ask good questions, to recognise a doubtful claim and to trace information back to a reliable source will be among the most useful skills of the coming decades. Machines can supply answers in abundance; deciding which of them deserve trust remains a human responsibility.

subject: English
q: The passage chiefly explains:
o: how vaccination protects communities as well as individuals
why vaccines are unsafe for newborn babies
how measles was eliminated throughout the world
why vaccination should remain a purely private matter
explanation: The passage explains herd immunity: when enough people are immune, a disease cannot spread, which protects the whole community.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, which of the following people depend on herd immunity for protection?
o: Adults who have been successfully vaccinated
Officials who organise vaccination campaigns
Patients whose weakened immune systems prevent vaccination
Travellers who bring in imported cases
explanation: The second paragraph lists patients with weakened immune systems, who cannot safely receive vaccines, among those who depend on others’ immunity.

subject: English
q: The passage mentions measles as an example of a disease that:
o: needs very high vaccination coverage to be controlled
cannot be prevented by any vaccine
affects only people with weak immune systems
no longer occurs anywhere in the world
explanation: Measles is cited as a highly contagious infection that requires very high coverage for herd immunity.

subject: English
q: The word ‘complacency’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: a careless feeling that there is no danger
deliberate hostility to modern medicine
a shortage of trained health workers
fear of an approaching epidemic
explanation: Complacency arises where a disease “has not been seen for years”, meaning people relax because they no longer sense any danger.

subject: English
q: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Herd immunity makes individual vaccination unnecessary
Every disease requires the same level of vaccination coverage
A person who refuses vaccination may endanger others as well as himself
Outbreaks can occur only where no one has been vaccinated
explanation: Because the vulnerable depend on the immunity of those around them and small falls in coverage open gaps, one person’s refusal affects others too.

subject: English
q: The author’s purpose in the final paragraph is to:
o: warn readers against the side effects of vaccines
describe how vaccines are manufactured
criticise officials for spreading rumours
present vaccination as a responsibility towards others
explanation: The last paragraph calls vaccination a civic act that builds a shield for the most vulnerable members of society.

subject: English
q: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?
o: Observation Against Theory: Tracing an Outbreak
The Invention of the Microscope
How Breweries Improved Public Health
Why Foul Air Causes Disease
explanation: The passage tells how careful observation of cases overturned the respectable theory of foul air, and its closing lesson is that theory must yield to observation.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, many nineteenth-century doctors believed that cholera was spread by:
o: contaminated water from public pumps
contact with brewery workers
insects breeding in crowded houses
foul air rising from rubbish and marshes
explanation: The first paragraph states that many doctors blamed foul air rising from rubbish and marshes.

subject: English
q: Why were some households far from the pump also affected?
o: They had fetched water from it because they liked its taste
The foul air had drifted into their streets
They worked at the nearby brewery
Their own wells were fed by the same drain
explanation: The physician found on inquiry that the distant households had drawn water from that pump because they preferred its taste.

subject: English
q: The fact that the brewery workers were mostly spared supported the physician’s view because they:
o: breathed cleaner air than their neighbours
had already been treated by other doctors
worked near the pump but did not rely on its water
lived far away from the affected district
explanation: The brewery was nearby, so the workers shared the district’s air, yet they drank largely what the brewery produced; their escape pointed to the water, not the air.

subject: English
q: The word ‘yield’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: give way
produce a profit
grow stronger
remain hidden
explanation: Theories “must yield to careful observation”, meaning they must give way when the evidence contradicts them.

subject: English
q: The author’s main purpose in the last paragraph is to:
o: criticise the physician for lacking proper instruments
describe how the pump was later repaired
explain the chemistry of contaminated water
draw a general lesson about evidence and theory
explanation: The final paragraph states that the episode carries a lesson beyond medicine: theories must yield to careful observation.

subject: English
q: The central point of the passage is that in the information age:
o: information has become too expensive for most people
attention, not information, has become the scarce resource
technology should be rejected as harmful
books have lost all their value
explanation: The first paragraph states that what has become scarce is not information but the attention needed to make sense of it.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why are websites and applications designed to hold our gaze?
o: They are required to do so by law
Their users ask for longer feeds
It helps readers concentrate for longer
They earn money when people look at them
explanation: The second paragraph says websites, applications and broadcasters earn money when people look at them.

subject: English
q: Which activity does the passage give as an example of one that needs sustained concentration?
o: Checking notifications as they arrive
Reading headlines written to provoke
Listening closely to another person
Scrolling through an endless feed
explanation: Reading a long argument, solving a difficult problem and listening closely to another person are the passage’s examples; the other options are the distractions it describes.

subject: English
q: The word ‘sinister’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: highly profitable
evil or threatening
purely accidental
overly complicated
explanation: The author says the design of digital media is not “necessarily sinister”, meaning not necessarily malicious, even though its effect is harmful.

subject: English
q: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: People in earlier centuries were more intelligent than people today
The design of digital media partly explains why concentration has become harder
Short and emotional information is always inaccurate
Notifications arrive at fixed and predictable times
explanation: Media are designed to capture attention with notifications, provocative headlines and endless feeds, and constant interruption makes sustained concentration harder.

subject: English
q: The author’s attitude towards modern technology is best described as:
o: appreciative but cautious
wholly hostile
uncritically enthusiastic
entirely indifferent
explanation: The author acknowledges the immense benefits of technology but warns about its effect on attention and urges deliberate use.

subject: English
q: The main idea of the passage is that AI writing tools:
o: understand language in the same way as human beings
are useful assistants whose output still requires human judgement
should be banned from schools and offices
have made human reasoning skills unnecessary
explanation: The author grants that the tools are useful but argues that their output can be false, so deciding what to trust remains a human task.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, these systems produce answers by:
o: consulting a panel of human experts
checking every claim against reliable sources
predicting which words are likely to follow others
copying complete essays from libraries
explanation: The first paragraph says they are trained on large collections of text and learn to predict which words are likely to follow others.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, when does the danger of these tools arise?
o: When programmers use them to find errors
When people treat them as an authority rather than an assistant
When they explain difficult ideas in simpler language
When a knowledgeable person reviews their output
explanation: The third paragraph states that the danger arises when people treat the technology as an authority rather than as an assistant.

subject: English
q: The word ‘plausible’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: seemingly reasonable or likely
certainly true
deliberately misleading
difficult to understand
explanation: The system generates what is statistically plausible, which can still be false; plausible means likely-seeming, not certainly true.

subject: English
q: The author suggests that the spread of AI tools will make human judgement more important because:
o: machines will soon refuse to answer difficult questions
the tools can produce convincing answers that may be false
the tools can only be operated by trained experts
people will have fewer sources of information than before
explanation: Since the tools generate confident, polished statements that may be wrong or cite invented sources, people must be able to recognise doubtful claims and check sources.

subject: English
q: The tone of the passage is best described as:
o: alarmed and hostile
playful and ironic
measured and advisory
boastful and promotional
explanation: The author calmly weighs the uses and limits of the technology and advises careful, critical use rather than rejection or praise.
